# Commandeck

> Commandeck is the universal remote for Jellyfin, Plex, Docker and your home server: a
> desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux that turns the commands you need into buttons.
> Click a button and the command runs — on this computer, or on your server over SSH — with
> the result shown in a window. It is built for people who want the benefits of a home server
> (NAS, mini-PC, Raspberry Pi, Proxmox or Docker box) without having to live in a terminal:
> instead of hunting again for a command buried in an old chat, a browser tab or a notes file,
> they press a button. No account, no cloud, no telemetry.

## What it is
- A grid of buttons, each one running a command you can read and edit.
- A native desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux) — not a web panel to host: nothing to install
  on the server, no container, no exposed port.
- Free, ready-made **button packs** for common setups, installed in one click from the app.
- An **Android** app (separate purchase, in closed testing before Google Play) that runs the
  same buttons on your machines over SSH, on your own network or your own VPN.

## Key facts
- Platforms: Windows 10/11, macOS (Apple Silicon), Linux (AppImage, x86-64 and ARM64).
- Free edition: unlimited buttons that run on this computer, all icons and colors, every pack.
- Pro ($29 one-time, lifetime — buy once, yours for good; 14-day free trial, no card, no
  account): buttons that reach your servers over SSH (password or key), one button on several
  machines at once, themes, backup and restore, saved "Run as" shortcuts, and an optional MCP
  server so an AI assistant can create and run buttons.
- Android: $19 one-time, paid on Google Play, no subscription.
- Button packs (all free, digitally signed, each written for one system): Jellyfin (Docker or
  system install), Plex (Docker or system install), Immich (Docker), Home Assistant (Docker),
  Home Server Starter (Docker), Batocera, plus Essentials, Hardware, Network and Developer Tools
  for Linux, macOS and Windows.
- Privacy: the app contacts nothing on its own. It talks to your own machines, to GitHub when
  you open the pack gallery or ask it to check for updates, and (desktop Pro only) to the
  payment provider to check a licence key. No account, no analytics, no crash reporting.
- Safety: every button shows its command before it runs; anything that restarts or deletes
  asks for confirmation; the admin (sudo) password is kept in the system keychain.

## Typical use cases
- Restart Jellyfin or Plex, make Plex look for new films, see why it uses all the CPU.
- Check disk space on a NAS before it fills up.
- Update a server, list and restart Docker containers, read their logs.
- Check a Home Assistant configuration before restarting it.
- Look after a Batocera retro-gaming box from the desk or the phone.
